utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, when we broke yesterday afternoon, I had been making some submissions to you by reference to the testimony of Rrustem Tetaj from the last trial concerning and a protected witness from this trial concerning Skender Kuqi and Mr. Haradinaj's intervention when the detention of Skender Kuqi was brought to his attention as the evidence establishes by Rrustem Tetaj himself. The first thing that he did was to make that difficult journey over to Jabllanice and then get there and remonstrate when he arrived with Nazmi Brahimaj over the treatment of Mr. Kuqi and order his immediate release, and Your Honours may remember the words from the protected witness that: This type of thing damages our cause. And Your Honours may think that this is a telling detail because of course, as I said to Your Honours yesterday, Mr. Haradinaj was commander of those who chose to follow him, and his popularity and the support that he and, indeed, the cause that he represented enjoyed within the community depended upon his reputation, and, to that extent, it may well be thought that the ill-treatment of those who have been detained, allegations of torture and the like of people in custody would have precisely the opposite effect, that which Mr. Haradinaj was so painstakingly seeking to build, namely a consensus among the community to take part in a volunteer force. So that was the first time he appears actively on the evidence in this case. There are two others. The second is in connection with Witness 3. Witness 3 Your Honours will recall was one of those who he said escaped from Jabllanice on the 17th, 18th July, and he testified in some considerable detail about being redetained, including, in the end, by Lahi Brahimaj and locked into the boot of a car and eventually delivered by Mr. Brahimaj to Glodjan where he was initially badly treated by a particular soldier there, and then two young boys who he believes to be the brothers, or one of them to be the brother of Mr. Haradinaj, entered the room, caused the ill-treatment to cease immediately and began altogether to treat him in a different manner. At that point, a man he believed to be Ramush Haradinaj, the commander of Glodjan certainly entered the room where he had been, and he told Your Honours that he was questioned by Mr. Haradinaj as to how he came to be there. He was then given -- offered food, given cigarettes, offered a bed for the night voluntarily, in other words, he was told he could stay the night if he wished to do so, but that he should sleep away from the window because there was a risk that otherwise he must be hit by a Serbian shell or sniper. In other words, as soon as Mr. Haradinaj arrived on the scene, he told, you his treatment was entirely appropriate, his presence was voluntary and he was given support. And I'm going to read a short passage of his testimony. He's asked this: "Q. So was it obvious to you as well that he, that is Mr. Haradinaj, didn't know who'd brought you there or what it was you were accused of?" This is transcript 1678, line 11 onwards. "A. I believe he was not aware, because it was a matter of time. When Mr. Lahi Brahimaj took me from the shop, there was no time to discuss with other people. I'm not sure, but I believe that he, that is Mr. Haradinaj, was not aware. "Q. And did you tell him that you were accused by Mr. Brahimaj of some form of treason? Did you tell the man you believed to be Mr. Haradinaj that that is what the accusation was or what did you say? "A. He asked me my name, where I was from, Who brought you here, and for what. I told him my name, surname, the name of my village. He asked, Why are you here? And I answered that there was a question of an automatic rifle. I was accused." Pausing there, Your Honours will recall that there was an allegation that Witness 3 of stolen a rifle that ought to have been surrendered to the KLA. The answer continues: "... he asked me whether I knew someone where I could sleep in Glodjan, and I said I didn't. "Q. Pause there because we'll come to the issue of where you were going to sleep in a moment or two. You've just told us that he asked you your name and where you were from and who brought you there and for what, and you say you told him your name, your surname, the name of your village, and he asked, Why are you here? And I answered there was a question of an automatic rifle. Now, pausing there, did you tell him that you had been brought there by Lahi Brahimaj? "A. Yes. "Q. How did he respond when you told him that? "A. He made this noise, shh," and it's recorded on the transcript as "shh," "It seemed incomprehensible to him, I think. "Q. What was the noise? Can you describe it for the record?" And then Your Honour Judge Moloto intervenes to say it's described on the record as "shh," and the witness says like this and then it's recorded p-w-o-w, "pwow." "... he was, I think," says the witness "angry, angry why these things happened, why these bad things happened." "Q. Angry towards whom do you think? "A. Of course that Lahi had taken me there." So, again, that witness in the evidence that he gave most certainly does not support the suggestion that any ill-treatment of him was pursuant to a joint criminal enterprise. Just as in the case of Skender Kuqi when ill-treatment was brought to Mr. Haradinaj's attention, the response was to remonstrate to criticise, to say this should never happen again, nothing of the kind should ever happen again because it is damaging our cause. So, too, when Witness 3 informs Mr. Haradinaj that he has been ill-treated, detained by Lahi Brahimaj in the way described, the reaction is that Mr. Haradinaj was angry why these bad things happened, angry towards Mr. Brahimaj. So that doesn't, in our submission, support a joint criminal enterprise. Indeed, it proves that no such joint criminal enterprise was in existence. This is not, I reiterate, a command responsibility case, but even if it were in the circumstances as they existed on the ground, it wouldn't begin, in our submission, to come close to the threshold necessary. But this is a joint criminal enterprise case, and what you have in each instance where there is an intervention by Mr. Haradinaj is an expression by those who saw it of what was clearly an attitude of opposition to the ill-treatment of individuals who had been detained at Jabllanice. Can we just move on to look at a short passage of video from Witness 3 where he deals with how he reacted to the treatment afforded to him by Mr. Haradinaj now.

I didn't know him. He didn't know me, and I am not afraid even now. "Q. But if that was what he was promising you, that no harm would come to you again, that is exactly with a happened, isn't it, Witness 3? No harm did come to you again after that. "A. That's correct. No harm came to me. No threats. I didn't have any contacts with them. "Q. And would it be fair to say that once you had come to the attention of Mr. Haradinaj, from that point onwards you were safe? "A. Yes. Yes, this is what had happened, in fact. I never had any problems."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want, if I may, to put on -- thank you. Now, just pausing there, I don't propose to say much by way of comment other than this: That it is perfectly clear from the testimony of Witness 3 that Mr. Haradinaj's intervention in his case was not only inconsistent with the existence or, rather, with the involvement of Mr. Haradinaj in a joint criminal enterprise to ill-treat Witness 3, but was proof positive of quite the reverse. Can I turn now to the third, and, in our submission, the last relevant evidence of an involvement of Mr. Haradinaj in this case, and that is the incident concerning the ECMM monitors that Mr. Rogers thought it right to place such reliance upon. Now I summarised to Your Honours yesterday what had happened in relation to that and when it had happened and pointed out that for the Prosecution to seek to rely on that interchange as evidence of Mr. Haradinaj's propensity for violence against those who were detained was, in the circumstances, preposterous. Mr. Pappas together with his interpreter, Kastriot, and two other ECMM monitors, one called Wolfgang Kaufmann and another individual present with him, had driven in a white Land Rover directly towards the confrontation that Your Honours saw yesterday depicted in the BBC news footage of the Serbian forces overrunning Glodjan and Irzniq causing wide scale destruction and the mass displacement of the civilian population. And there was initially a situation where they were stopped by armed men as they approached Irzniq, taken to a KLA headquarters. There was a confrontation in which the interpreter initial was struck and the interpreter then told Mr. Pappas that these armed man who are unidentified suspected that they were spies for the Serbs. They had, as the evidence disclosed, satellite telephones and maps with them. After about 25 minutes, he said, Mr. Haradinaj arrived. He asked them some questions, but as Mr. Pappas told the last Trial Chamber, it was totally different the way he was behaving, the way he was asking information. Once Mr. Haradinaj arrived, everything was quite civilised. Yet again, once Mr. Haradinaj arrived, everything was quite civilised. That's P318, transcript T4132. Once Mr. Pappas, explained that this was an ECMM group, Mr. Haradinaj was quite open and understood their mission. Not only that, but having been called away from the front line to deal with this somewhat reckless escapade by the ECMM group, Mr. Haradinaj took them back to their car, checked that it wasn't concealing weapons, told them that they were free to leave and arranged for them to be escorted safely out of the area. And Mr. Pappas, when asked, said that throughout this encounter Mr. Haradinaj was "absolutely calm and controlled" and that his manner was "gentle and polite." Now, just pause for a moment on this, if I may, because what Your Honours have in the evidence is a 92 ter witness statement of Mr. Pappas, but in the original trial he had signed, first of all, a much more detailed consolidated witness statement which contained the passage explaining just how appropriately Mr. Haradinaj had behaved during his intervention. That passage did not, however, find its way into the 92 ter statement. And, accordingly, he was cross-examined on the passage that had not found its way into the 92 ter statement that Your Honours have. And it may be, I don't know, that in proposing that this was relevant evidence in this case of Mr. Haradinaj's propensity for violence that the Prosecution overlooked this. Certainly had they focused on it, it would have been very difficult for them to make the submission that they made. Can we look, please, now at a short passage of video in which he was cross-examined, Mr. Pappas, about that section and what he had to say about it. This is P397.

utterances.text: "Q. ... to you and ask you, please, to confirm that these are an accurate reflection of your evidence because they don't find their way into the written statement that has been admitted in evidence in this case. Quotation - and I'm reading from the second half of paragraph 24 of the consolidated witness statement and then on: "'He was absolutely calm and controlled, and in a gentle way he started interrogating us one by one. He was polite. He started with Penti, who was obviously shocked, frightened from the development of things, Penti' and this is in brackets, '(Penti had been visiting our team for just that day and this had happened to him)' closed brackets, full stop. 'He checked his papers and only had a short discussion with him. I recall that he asked Penti a question about a lake if Finland that was the subject of some dispute with the Russians and Penti answered him. After Penti, he asked the interpreter in Albanian a few things; however, I'm not aware about the content of their conversation. After Kastriot, he turned to me and asked me about my whereabouts and occupation back home. He told me that he has no problem with Greeks, although the politics of my country build up hostile feelings in a lot of his comrades. He told me that he had visited Greece several times and that he has a lot of Albanian friends living there and some of them came to Kosovo to fight with him. I explained to him the circumstances in which we had ended up there, meaning our presence in Rznic. I explained to him our mandate and the purpose of our presence in Kosovo. It seemed to me that he understood and was satisfied with my explanations. Afterwards, he spoke in French and English with Kaufmann.' "And then a little further on at paragraph 26, I want to put the following passage on the record: "'Afterwards, the commander came with us to our car and he started to search it thoroughly inside and outside. He asked us if we had guns and we said no. After this, he told us that we are free to go. He offered us an escort out of the area which we agreed to. He then ordered the three men in the black uniform, including Idriz Balaj, who had stopped us before, to escort us out of Glodjan.' "And then, finally, two lines at the bottom of paragraph 26: "'The whole incident lasted for about one and a half hours under continuous shelling of Serbian artillery.' "So, first of all, can I ask you, please, to confirm that that is an accurate reflection of your evidence? "A. Yes, it is. "Q. And secondly, just one or two supplementary questions. It follows from that description that your impression of Mr. Haradinaj was that he remained calm throughout this interchange and behaved reasonably to you. Is that right? "A. That's right. "Q. And this was despite the fact that the village of Glodjan and the village of Rznic were under heavy fire and the Serbs were closing in? "A. They were under shelling, yes. I don't know, it's out estimation that the Serbs were very close, yes. "Q. And you know from the video you saw yesterday that by the following day they'd overrun Glodjan? "A. Yeah. "Q. Now, for a commander to come away from the front line, to divert himself and others from combat to deal with a group of monitors who had decided to drive straight into the heart of a front line zone, would you accept it's obviously a rather unwelcome distraction from the job of defending people's lives in the course of the conflict? "A. In the way that you put it, yes. "Q. But nonetheless, once he had established your good faith, he not only returned your documents and ensured that you could leave but gave you safe passage out of the area, diverting soldiers again -- "JUDGE ORIE: Mr. Emmerson, I have to ask you to slow down for the interpreters. "MR. EMMERSON: Sorry. "JUDGE ORIE: Could you perhaps please repeat your last question. "MR. EMMERSON: "Q. I said: Nonetheless, once he established your good faith, he not only returned your documents and ensured that you could leave but gave you safe passage out of the area, again diverting soldiers from the front line to meet the needs of providing you with protection. "A. Exactly."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, how can it be that a responsible Prosecutor would put that incident forward as evidence of Mr. Haradinaj's supposed involvement in a joint criminal enterprise to ill-treatment prisoners in Jabllanice? Those three incidents, Mr. Haradinaj's intervention in Skender Kuqi's case, his intervention in the case of Witness 3, and his intervention in the case of the ECMM monitors are the only evidence in this trial of his active involvement in anything apart from the confrontation with FARK soldiers which I'm going to come back to towards the end of my submissions, but leaving the FARK distraction to one side where it belongs, those three incidents are the only evidence of Mr. Haradinaj doing anything relevant in this case and what do they tell us? A joint criminal enterprise? I don't think so. What then of the sloppy allegation that simply because he was a popular KLA commander he must be guilty? That's really what it comes to. It's necessary to put that in its proper context. Mr. Rogers tried to dismiss the consistent evidence that was before this Trial Chamber and the last that there was no vertical command structure even after the 23rd of June. Mr. Emmerson might call it horizontal, but in the end he was an influential commander. Well, we're to the dealing with abstractions and generalities of that nature in a criminal trial. We deal in specifics. And there are no specifics upon which Mr. Rogers is in a position to rely, but let's just look at what the evidence was. Can I just show Your Honours, first of all, the evidence of Skender Rexhametaj, who Mr. Rogers relies upon and sought to put before you to suggest that this relationship was such that Mr. Haradinaj can somehow be held responsible for what happened in Jabllanice. This is -- this is tab 10 in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Q. ... yesterday that until the 23rd of June meeting you personally of never received an order from Ramush Haradinaj. You were subzone commanders of equal rank even though he was your co-ordinator, you told us yesterday, and you never received an order from him before the 23rd of June. Do you remember telling us that yesterday? "A. Yes. I remember that, and that stands. I told you that everything that was done was done on the basis of -- "Q. I'm going to suggest to you that that remained the position after the 23rd of June, that you never received an order from Ramush Haradinaj to do or not to do anything militarily within your subzone after the 23rd of June. "A. Yes. The subzones and the responsibilities of the subzone commanders continued. We continued to work on functionalising the positions and the responsibilities even after the 23rd of June. "Q. And in practical terms, after the 23rd of June the relationship between the subzone commanders, in practical terms, remained horizontal? "A. Yes, it remained horizontal in reality, which means that no one could give orders to the other. Everything was done by consensus. It remained the same."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So prior to the 23rd of June it is common ground and unequivocally established that Jabllanice existed wholly outside the four subzones that had been established on the 26th of May and after the 23rd of June the relationship between the commanders, both within and outside that subzone, that's to say those that formed the Dukagini Plain Operational Zone remained horizontal in reality "which means that no one could give orders to the other." You see when, Mr. Rogers makes the concession, as he does, that this was a force with no conventional command structure, he fails to take that through to its logical conclusion. The logical conclusion is that this was not an army with a vertical hierarchy at all precisely because it depended on the consensus of volunteers, people who were culturally, you've heard, centred around loyalty to their own villages and their elected village heads. It was necessary for everything to be debated by consensus, typically in the oda where men would gather and debate what should be done. There was no suggestion that there was any debate at any stage which resulted in a decision to detain, beat, or kill people in Jabllanice or indeed to establish a detention facility there. So Mr. Rogers says, Well, we've got a witness from the first trial called Zymer Hasanaj who says that Ramush Haradinaj appointed a commander in Vranoc. Remember I showed Your Honours Vranoq. It was near Baran and one of the villages attacked in the May offensive. I said you may want to note Vranoq. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's better. E-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So subzone 1, this is the 26th of May meeting. Subzone 1 around Glodjan, this is Rrustem Tetaj's map; subzone 2, Irzniq under the command of Rrustem Tetaj; subzone 3, the area around Pozar and Dasinovac under the command of Skender Rexhahmetaj, who you've just seen testifying about horizontal structures throughout; and subzone 4 under the command of Shemsedin Cekaj, who also gave evidence in trial one about the horizontal relationships that existed. And it -- it doesn't take me to make the point that Jabllanice falls well outside of that subzone structure. So we know that from the beginning of the indictment period right up to the 23rd of June, Jabllanice was even formally entirely outside any attempts at co-ordination of these zones along the front line. What we also know from the evidence you've just heard is even after the 23rd of June there was no command relationship of the short that Mr. Rogers has tried to conjure up. So what did the witnesses say about this? First of all, Mr. Tetaj himself explaining his map -- can we please -- this is tab 13, just call up a short passage of Mr. Tetaj's evidence. P521.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Q. ... more detail at the minutes of the meeting that took place in Jabllanice on the 23rd of June; but, first of all, we can see from the zones that you've marked on this map that as at the end of May, they did not include any area to the west of the main road. Is that correct?"

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you may wonder why we're -- what I hear from the video here is not what I see on the transcript at tab 13. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we just -- can we just try again because I think it may be that it cut in at the wrong moment because it certainly seems to be what I put on my transcript. Is Your Honour's transcript -- is it headed 3720, beginning, "I'm going to ..."?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's correct, "I'm going to ...," yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think that -- I think that unless I'm mistaken, I think that is the passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "Q. I'm going to come back in a little while and look in more detail at the minutes of the meeting that took place in Jabllanice on the 23rd of June, but, first of all, we can see from the zones that you've marked on this map that as at the end of May, they did not include any area to the west of the main road. Until the moment when the original staff of Dukagjin was set up, Jabllanice was a separate zone so it was not included in these four subzones. It was not included in them. "Q. Well, that was what I wanted to ask you. You say until the -- the translation which 'the original staff of Dukagjin was set up.' Can I just be clear. Are you saying until the meeting on the 23rd of June when the staff of the Dukagjini Plain was established, until then, Jabllanice was not part of this co-ordinated grouping? Is that right? "A. That's correct. That's correct."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And can we just run now through a series of testimonies back to back, and I'll explain what they are with even of them just before they start. So the next tab 13 -- I'm sorry 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, can I have -- can I ask a little question. The area Hasanaj in tab 11 he's talking about, could you remind me of which subzone that is in?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Vranoq, if Your Honour sees Baran, outside -- it's on in amongst the subzones, it's outside as well. If you look at Baran, which is just to the upper right-hand corner of subzone 4 -- yes, I'm sorry. Baran outside, but Vranoq, if you look beneath immediately south of Vranoq it's just in the edge of the subzone 3 under the command of Shemsedin Cekaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So, as I say, I'm just going to run through these passages and just introduce them as we go. So tab 14 is the evidence of Skender Rexhametaj on the way in which relationships operated between these different villages. Can we just look at that briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Q. And so -- and so would you agree with me that one of the reasons why a commander from subzone -- from a particular subzone could not impose his will on another subzone was because everybody was volunteering and everything had to be agreed by consent? "A. Yes, correct. "Q. But there was also another reason which you told us about right at the beginning of your testimony yesterday in some detail, which is that these areas, these -- these -- these concentrations, these towns and villages where commanders had been appointed, were fiercely, culturally jealous of their independence from one another. Would you agree with that? "A. I would kindly ask you to repeat the question. "Q. Another reason why everything had to be done by consensus was because culturally in Western Kosovo - as you told us yesterday - these towns, which were concentrations of KLA activity were fiercely jealous of their independence. They protected their independence from one another. They wouldn't want another leader from another town telling them what to do because that would break the consensus, wouldn't it? "A. It's correct, because these people who were appointed -- who were appointed through the will of the local people going through the rounds I mentioned. So the arrival of everyone else to command, to take over the command, was -- didn't make sense to them. So I think they wouldn't agree. I believe they wouldn't have liked that, because they trusted us and I believe that we did a good job, given that the objective circumstances. "Q. Now, just to conclude, in your evidence as a whole, we've really talked about six subzones, the four that were marked on the map I showed you by Rrustem Tetaj, the one that you've told us about that's on the western side of the road around Voksh, subzone 5, and the zone surrounding Jabllanice, which I think is sometimes referred to as Dushaka -- is that correct? Dushkaja. I'm sorry. "A. Yes, yes. That's right. "Q. And even after the 23rd of June, right up, let us say, until the end of September, it was not possible, was it, for the commander of any one of those zones to march into another one and tell the people there what to do and what not to do as an order? "A. Unless it was asked for, otherwise it was not possible. "Q. And that remains the position despite this aspirational blueprint that we see on the screen in front of us, didn't it? "A. Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the aspiration blueprint were the minutes of the meeting on the 23rd of June on which Mr. Rogers relies. Next, please, Bizlim Zyrapi trying to explain to the Trial Chamber the cultural issues underlying this independence. This is tab 15 and there are two short passages I want to play, please. Tabs 15 and 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Q. I'm sorry for that diversion, Mr. Zyrapi, we were going through the relationships between the military power bases that were associated with the main families in Western Kosovo. And you've told us it would be absurd to suggest that either the Brahimajs or the Haradinajs could tell the Jasharis what to do or what not to do inside their compound and you've told us it would be absurd to suggest that the Brahimajs could tell the Haradinajs what to do or what not to do inside their compound. And the last question which is the obvious concomitant of the first three: It would be absurd, would it not, to suggest that the Haradinajs were in a position to tell the Brahimajs at that point in time what to do and what not to do? "MR. MENON: Your Honour, it's the same problem. There is no basis for that question being put to this particular witness. It's not clear to me how he can comment on that particular family tie that Mr. Emmerson is referring to, the Haradinaj-Brahimaj family tie. "JUDGE MOLOTO: I'm sure the witness can tell us if he's not able to comment on that tie. Overruled. "MR. EMMERSON: "Q. It would be absurd, wouldn't it, Mr. Zyrapi, to suggest that in March 1998 the Haradinaj family could impose their will or discipline on what was or was not done by the Brahimajs inside Jabllanice? "A. [No interpretation]"

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, pausing there, that "jo," that "no" on the transcript is capable of being ambiguous because of Mr. Menon's interruption in the testimony. The actual question was, It would be absurd, wouldn't it, to suggest that Mr. Haradinaj could tell Mr. Brahimaj what to do. And the answer on the transcript actually says "no" and the inference obviously was that what the witness meant to say was, Yes, it would be absurd, no, he couldn't do it. But we clarified that immediately afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Q. Mr. Zyrapi, I want to suggest to you that in March 1998 none of these three families had authority to impose their will on one another. That is correct, is it not? "A. I wasn't there at that period to be able to know, but experience would show that, yes, that is correct. "Q. Thank you."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, pausing there, we're going to move on now to a witness that Mr. Rogers cited to you yesterday in support of certain aspects of the evidence about command. Cufe Krasniqi, who gave evidence in the first trial and there were two passage I want to -- I want to play Your Honours. They're both very brief. Essentially, his testimony was to the effect that these commands remained separate not solely after the 23rd of June but right through to the end of July; in other words, to the time just before the August offensive. Can we play, first of all, tab 17 which is P514.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Q. When you were answering questions about this relationship between these different power centres in the period after the 11th of July yesterday, you said they were not linked. You said: 'In Glodjan there was Ramush. In Prapaqan it was Tahir. Each operated independently, which means that we did not have the means and the possibilities to communicate with each other.' Then you said: 'However, if there was a problem or if we wanted to send some information, we send a courier in order to ask for some help.' And then you said this: 'When I was in Baran, if I had some problems, then I send some soldier with a vehicle in order to ask for some help. I sent him to Ramush, to Lahi, or to Tahir, the one which was closer.' "And I wanted to understand that answer a little more. Are you telling the Trial Chamber that from where you were in Vranoq, any one of those three commanders would be regarded from your point of view as operating autonomously so that you could call them or contact them directly? "A. Yes. That was not important at the time. If a village came under attack, all the villages voluntarily offered to help. So, for example, when the attack began on Jabllanice, I asked for assistance from other villages, because Ramush could not come from Glodjan to the place where I was. So whichever village was able to send volunteers to help, they would do so. "Q. And what you appear to be describing is a fairly horizontal, rather than vertical, command structure. Would you accept that description? "A. Yes, that's true. That's what happened. It's something that really happened. Whichever villages were closer to where the attack occurred, those villages went to assist."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And now tab 18, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Q. And again so that we're clear, during this month of July, there had been a major Serb offensive, a major battle at Loxha in the first -- the end of the first week of July. Is that correct? "A. Not in the last week of July, earlier. "Q. [Previous translation continues]... that may have been a translation issue. The end of the first week of July was what I was putting to you. "A. Yes, end of the first week. "Q. [Previous translation continues]... "A. I think you're right. About the 5th or 6th. "Q. And there was another major Serb offensive through the area within a week or so of the swearing-in ceremony, wasn't there? "A. Yes, there was. "Q. ... just important to get our chronology clear. Now, looking at this map you've told us it's depicting in a graphic way the locations after the 10th or 12th of July, and we can see that you've described Jabllanice as a staff HQ, and you described Glodjan as a staff HQ. And I just wanted to understand from your perspective as an officer on the ground in Baran, is that how you saw them as being on an equal footing and independent of one another, those two staff HQs? "A. Yes. At that moment, this was how it was. They were independent. The same was true of us. We had no means and each of us operated independently."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So that date's important because he's saying after the battle ended on the 12th of July, they remained independent. So that's a full three weeks following the 23rd of June minutes, but it's a position he's describing going forwards after the 12th of July. Of course, that was the very period where on the evidence Pal Krasniqi, Skender Kuqi, Witness 3 and Witness 6 were detained at Jabllanice and a few days before the escape attempt of which you have heard evidence. And so we're left in this situation that in the absence of anything specific to rely on, the Prosecution falls back on reputational evidence, that slippery dangerous area of inference based on nothing but tittle tattle. And you get a curiosity here, because in Mr. Balaj's case they rely on evidence suggesting - some of it from the Serbian intelligence - that Mr. Balaj had a fearsomely bad reputation. That alone. So therefore he must be guilty. Whereas in Mr. Haradinaj's case, quite the opposite thing is said. He had an incredibly good reputation and was hugely popular and therefore he must be guilty. That's the danger of this type of slippery unevidenced reasoning, but let's look at whether it's fair what Mr. Rogers put to you. Let's look at whether -- try to derive from the testimony of people in Western Kosovo who thought that Ramush Haradinaj was a war hero who protected them, a man who didn't engage in dirty abuse, an honourable fighter, how it is that the Prosecution seeks to turn that into evidence from which I invite you to infer a joint criminal enterprise. Can we start at tab 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Q. Did Ramush visit your brigade a couple of -- on a couple of occasions there, accompanied by Sali Veseli and Idriz Balaj? "A. Ramush came but Balaj was not with him. I did not see him. He was not there. Sali came on his own and Ramush came on his own. "Q. What was the purpose of the oath-taking ceremony in July 1998? "A. The aim of the visit was because we had made a request to him. We had a great number of soldiers that wanted to join the KLA, and we wanted them to pledge their allegiance and we wanted him to be present in this ceremony so that he could see from close what these young men were doing and how they were so eager to join the KLA. "Q. Who's the 'he'? You're referring to Ramush Haradinaj there? "A. Yes, of course, Ramush. We invited him and we wanted him to be part of that solemn ceremony, in the oath-taking ceremony of the new members of the brigade. "Q. Why was it so important to you that Ramush participated in this? "A. It was important because people loved him. People wanted to see him and to get to know him from close by, because for them, Ramush was an idol and he still is. "Q. Did they see him as a strong, powerful commander? "MR. EMMERSON: I appreciate Mr. Re may not be getting the answer he wants, but to seek to put words in the witness's mouth through the form of leading questions, in my submission, is not an appropriate course. Let him ask the witness questions in a non-leading form and have the answers that he gets. "JUDGE ORIE: Mr. Re, could you reformulate the question or put another question to the witness. "MR. RE: "Q. You said a moment ago that for people Ramush was an idol. Why did they see him as a idol? "A. I don't know. That's what people thought. They trusted Ramush and they thought that he was a person who sacrificed his own family to protect the whole population, and that's why he was considered an idol. So he was not ready to sacrifice only himself but his whole family. "Q. What was the feedback you were getting from these people about Ramush's command style? "A. Ramush had no time to command everywhere, but people trusted him. They thought that if Ramush went there, there would be no problem for them, for the people. This is something that occurred among the people. That's how the people loved him."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rogers read to you an extract from the evidence of Skender Rexhametaj on this question of Mr. Haradinaj's authority, but -- but he -- he read only one passage and I'm going to show you two, because they're put in proper context. First the one that Mr. Rogers read to you in his closing speech. This is tab 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Q. Sir, I'll repeat the question for you. Can you tell us, sir, whether KLA soldiers in the Dukagjin Zone respected Ramush Haradinaj's authority and I'm referring to the time period from -- from prior to the 23rd of May, 1998, and after the 23rd of May, 1998."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry we've jumped forward I'm afraid. Tab 20 it should be, first of all, which is from the transcript of Mr. Rexhametaj's evidence in this trial at 1097. [Microphone not activated]... video in that section, so I'll just read the transcript. This is Mr. Menon asking about a passage in

utterances.speaker: MR. REXHAMETAJ'S WITNESS STATEMENT
utterances.text: "A. The fourth sentence of the Albanian version of my statement should correspond to the English version which reads, 'Prior to the 23rd of June ... he already had de facto authority over the Dukagini zone.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS' POINT
utterances.text: "... and I don't think," says Mr. Menon, "that there's any dispute that the 'he' you're referring to is Ramush Haradinaj. Can you tell me, sir, what you meant by the word 'authority'? "A. I meant that based on the resistance that he put up with his family, the incident had a lot of echo in the whole country and Ramush as a result of that was widely respected for this resistance that he put up in protecting his family and his village. And with the passage of time, in fact, he became famous. Everyone -- most of the people knew him and had a lot of respect for him, because, as I said, he put up that resistance and protected his family and his village. This is my way of thinking when I said that. "Q. ... sorry, sir, continue," says Mr. Menon. "A. So on the basis of what I just said people respected him and ... if you're respected you enjoy authority ... I don't mean here legal authority but the authority of a person who was successful in protecting his family and his village and his people. This is my line of thinking."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So "authority" there is being misused by the Prosecution in their closing submission. This is not any form of authority over other people. This is authority in the sense that people respected Mr. Haradinaj for what he had done, but let's look at how Mr. Rexhametaj then goes on to explain it a little later. This is 1099. It's tab 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Q. Sir, I'll repeat the question for you. Can you tell us, sir, whether KLA soldiers in the Dukagjin Zone respected Ramush Haradinaj's authority? And I'm referring to the time period from -- from prior to the 23rd of May, 1998, and after the 23rd of May, 1998 -- or, excuse me, after the 23rd of June, 1998, it should read. "A. The population always respected him. The population was suffering. Ordinary people were suffering, and he defended them. So that's why they respected him. "Q. And my question actually was specific to KLA soldiers, sir. "A. The whole population -- "Q. Okay. Thank you, sir. "A. -- wanted defence and they got it. "Q. Okay. Thank you very much, sir. And can you elaborate, sir, for us on why Mr. Haradinaj was appointed as the commander of the Dukagjin Zone officially on the 23rd of June, 1998? Why was he selected? "A. Because we proposed him. "Q. Why did you propose him? "A. Perhaps we were not sure that we, the others, could carry that duty upon our shoulders. That's why we proposed him. He had shown what he could do and we proposed him. Ramush could have refused, but he took on the responsibility by respecting us and our proposal. He -- out of his goodwill, he accepted the task, but he could have refused. "Q. And, sir, when you say 'he had shown what he could do,' can you clarify what you mean by that, sir? "A. I mentioned it earlier. He had shown that he was a good soldier, a good leader, and a person who could gather people around him; and that's why we decided that Ramush be a co-ordinator for the subzones earlier. The same logic worked later. There were five professional officers there, and each of us could have taken that burden upon their shoulders, but we proposed him, and he did not hesitate. He respected our will and our proposal for him to be the leader. "Q. And, sir, when you say that Ramush Haradinaj was a person who could gather people around him, what do you mean by that, sir? "A. I mean that he knew how to respect other people. He was a good communicator. He was reasonable. So this was a person who could gather people around himself. It was this that I meant. He was able to discuss the problems that people had with them. He listened to their concerns and that's why he had that reputation."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's one final passage I want to deal very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that not be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Simply that I'm reaching the end of the topic and I'm happy to break and do one section after the break or do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Simply as regards that last passage, obviously Your Honours have seen that the testimony is that Mr. Haradinaj gathered people around him because he was reasonable, knew how to respect them and listened to their concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, we have heard, we have seen that. Just do the last thing that you've said you wanted to do before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Tab 22, please. This is Zymer Hasanaj from the first trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "Q. In paragraph 5, you refer to an expression: 'God in heaven; Ramush on earth,' meaning that he had great authority. Then you say, 'No one was superior to him.' "I just want you to tell the Trial Chamber, the Judges, what you mean by 'no one was superior to' Ramush. "A. I -- I said this because from -- every time there was a Serb attack until the KLA became engaged in the war, when the name became known, Ramush -- that of Ramush Haradinaj, it was myself who put that expression, 'God in heaven; Ramush on earth.' "Q. What do you mean by 'no one was superior to him'? "A. I thought that -- how can you put up a resistance to the enemy. I didn't know that it was difficult to put up resistance. In fact, it was very small resistance that was put up. "Q. I'm not sure I quite understand your answer. I'm asking you about why you say that no one was superior to him. What do you mean by 'superior to' Ramush? "A. After his -- he became known, I don't know how it has been translated there, but I personally gave this description. It was my personal opinion. "Q. And what do you -- what do you mean by it? That's what I'm asking you: What do you mean by 'no one was superior to him'? "A. He was good then and he's good now -- I mean, he's loved by people. He's considered -- he is -- he's held in esteem by the Albanian people."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That would be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wonder if I may now to turn to the evidence that you've heard concerning those people who were detained at Jabllanice and what they say about whether they did or did not see Ramush Haradinaj there at any time and what can be inferred from that. First of all, you heard testimony of from Witnesses 75 and 76 in connection with the detention of their relative who they said was detained on several occasions but was held for a considerable period up until the end of May and that they visited the compound on numerous occasions and saw various members of the staff there, and they both stated in terms that they never saw Mr. Haradinaj in Jabllanice on any of those visits. That's transcript 1845 and P304, the witness 76 92 ter statement at paragraph 13. Witness 75 stated that it was Lahi Brahimaj who was in charge of Jabllanice during the period he went there and accurately that Mr. Haradinaj was not yet commander of the Dukagjin area. The testimony of Shefqet Kabashi that was admitted in these proceedings from the Limaj trial, he said that he had been based in Jabllanice as a KLA soldier consistently from April through to September 1998, and his evidence was that there was, during the whole of that time, no one in a more senior position to Lahi Brahimaj in command of Jabllanice, and there is no suggestion whatever in that testimony that during the whole of that time he ever saw Mr. Haradinaj anywhere in Jabllanice. Now, we know he did go to two formal meetings there. We know he did go to intervene on Skender Kuqi's behalf, and we know that he did go on one occasion, according to Witness 80 at least, when he was surrounded by other people and there were villagers present in the staff in the main part of the village, not the so-called detection facility. But Kabashi never saw him there. So the suggestion that Mr. Rogers tried to make that Mr. Haradinaj was a regular visitor doesn't appear on its face to be consistent with the testimony of any of those witnesses. But what about Witness 3? Witness 3 was on his evidence detained at Jabllanice for a considerable period of time, escaped, was taken back there. And of course he came across Ramush Haradinaj for the first time when he got to Glodjan, and after that, as we've seen, nothing ever happened to him again. In other words, he did not see Mr. Haradinaj at Jabllanice. What about Witness 6? Witness 6 is significant because as Your Honours know, he was detained for six weeks from the 13th of June, and his testimony, which has been admitted, is -- is that a day after the escape on the 18th or 19th of July, he was freed within the confines of the compound. In other words, he was -- to all intents and purposes, by appearance he was working in the kitchens and free to move around the compound, albeit that he was still detained. So it's not as though he was locked in a room where he wouldn't have been able to see anybody coming or going. He would have seen all comings and goings in and out of the compound. Let me read you his testimony from trial 1. This is page 5391. He's asked about when Skender Kuqi goes to hospital, and he says: "A. I don't know. I didn't see him. But when I took bread to Pal Krasniqi, he," Skender Kuqi, "wasn't there any more. "Q. And might that have been a day or two after the escape attempt that you've described?" And he says: "One day after. "Q. And from that point onwards, just so that we have the picture, once again, there was only one person in detention, namely Pal Krasniqi; is that correct? "A. Yes. "Q. You were still not free to leave, but to external appearances you were wandering around the yard and washing the dishes and so forth; is that right? "A. That's right." And then a little further down: "Q. And just one final question on timing before I ask you one or two other matters. Do you know how long it was after your -- you got your relative freedom that the man from Zahaq arrived. "A. One or two days after that, I can't be very precise. "Q. Thank you. What I want to do now is just put one or two passages to you, Witness 6, from first of all the witness statement that you made in February and March 2004. That was the statement that you made when you were shown some photographic line-ups, and you were shown a line-up of photographs that included a photograph of Ramush Haradinaj. I won't bother to pull it up on the screen, but I'm just going to read to you the passage from the witness statement that you have signed and ask you to confirm that it is correct. Having been shown the photograph which was a line-up including a photograph of Mr. Haradinaj you said this, and I'm quoting from your statement at paragraph 3: "'I can identify Ramush Haradinaj. While his face has become familiar to me after the war from several newspaper articles and television programmes, I did not know him from the time of the war and cannot remember seeing him in the KLA prison in Jabllanice.' "I'll ask you, please, to confirm that that is a correct statement of your evidence. "A. Yes." So Witness 3, who was there for six weeks and moving freely around the compound from -- I'm sorry, Witness 6. Did I say 3? I do apologise. And moving freely around the walled compound from around about the 18th of July, he never saw Ramush Haradinaj there either. And so we are left with Mr. Rogers' speculative theory as the only evidence that the Prosecution can point to connecting Ramush Haradinaj to any of these crimes, and the theory goes like this: You can be sure from the testimony of the protected witness that the three boys were arrested and taken to Jabllanice prior to the attacks by the Serb forces on Grabanice, and you can be sure that the occasion when the protected witness saw Ramush Haradinaj surrounded by a group of men inside the staff took place after the attack on Grabanica, probably a week after. Therefore, they must have been in detention all the way through at Jabllanice, and even though the protected witness didn't say that he saw them there that day, the Prosecution say Mr. Haradinaj must have known that they were there, and therefore, the Prosecution say, he must be complicit in the joint criminal enterprise. That's, as I've understood it, is the way that Mr. Rogers is finally driven to put his case. The short answer is this: Whilst one cannot but admire the forensic ingenuity with which he sought painstakingly to build the elaborate edifice of inference that he's invite you go to draw, its foundations rest on sand. First of all, Your Honours are going to have to read the testimony of the protected witness with care, because as regards the dates, the days and the occasions, he was multiply inconsistent. The suggestion, and it's made in the Prosecution brief at para 211 quotes: "There can be no uncertainty that the Count 1 victims were executed after Haradinaj's visit." Simply cannot be derived on any rational view from a reading of the testimony of the protected witness as a whole. He said in clear terms when asked directly about the timing of those two incidents that the incidents with the 20 or 30 villagers took place before the ear cutting incident had occurred. That's T2414. He then underscored that by making it clear on several occasions that the incident with the villagers took place after the Serb attack on Grabanice but that the incident with the boys being arrested and detained took place before that. Now, Your Honours punctured the myth with a simple question in the course of Mr. Rogers' submission: Do we know on the evidence when the boys were taken to Jabllanice? Answer from Mr. Rogers: No, we do not. That is the end of the matter. Because unless the Prosecution could prove that beyond reasonable doubt, the date on which the boys were taken to Jabllanice, they couldn't begin to invite you to return a conclusion that they must have been there on the day that Mr. Haradinaj was there with the 20 or 30 villagers. That's the end of it. But even if it weren't the end of it, and even if they were there, and even if it was possible to draw that inference, the protected witness didn't see them there, so why should Mr. Haradinaj have seen them there? Because the protected witness and Mr. Haradinaj were in the same building, the staff, in another part of Jabllanice. So how can Mr. Rogers suggest that Mr. Haradinaj must have known that they were there when the protected witness himself -- if -- even on Mr. Rogers' completely speculative theory, didn't know that they were there at that time. The fact of the matter is that -- that -- and I'm going to invite Your Honours to -- and it will need to be done with care, to go through each and every time when the witness tried to locate the dates of occasions and you will see that they are wholly inconsistent the one with the other. So for example, he -- there is a reference to a village called Bucan in the evidence and to detentions having taken -- perhaps this part I ought to do in private session, in fact.

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Emmerson, the Chamber did say it's not going to impose time limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm moving to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
